item.text:
The HVAC demand flexibility measures are **upgrades 24–28** in ResStock 2025 Release 1. They vary by control strategy, thermostat offset, and adjustment duration. The release’s [Upgrade Measures page](https://natlabrockies.github.io/ResStock.github.io/docs/upgrade_measures.html) identifies all five:

| Upgrade | Strategy | Duration of adjustment | Thermostat change |
|---|---|---|---|
| **24** | On-peak load shedding | 4 hours during peak | Heating **−2°F**; cooling **+2°F** |
| **25** | Pre-peak load shifting | 4 hours before peak | Preheat **+2°F**; precool **−2°F** |
| **26** | On-peak load shedding | 4 hours during peak | Heating **−4°F**; cooling **+4°F** |
| **27** | Pre-peak load shifting | 4 hours before peak | Preheat **+4°F**; precool **−4°F** |
| **28** | Pre-peak load shifting | 1 hour before peak | Preheat **+2°F**; precool **−2°F** |

The durations and offsets are confirmed in [*ResStock Measure Documentation: HVAC Load Flexibility*, Table 8, p. 25](https://docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy26osti/93846.pdf#page=33).

**Shedding** reduces heating or cooling demand during peak hours by allowing indoor temperature to drift toward a less comfortable setpoint. Upgrade 26 uses twice the offset of upgrade 24.

**Shifting** preheats or precools the home, using its thermal mass to reduce subsequent peak-period demand. Upgrade 27 doubles upgrade 25’s offset; upgrade 28 shortens the preconditioning period from four hours to one. These shifting scenarios have **no on-peak setpoint adjustment**, and the shedding scenarios have **no preconditioning**. The final measures do not combine both strategies. [Report, §1.2, p. 3, and §4.4, p. 25](https://docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy26osti/93846.pdf).

Peak windows vary by state and season; the modeling derives them from projected 2050 net loads. The measures apply to homes with heating or cooling—approximately **99.7% of the stock**. [Report, pp. 1, 5–7](https://docs.nlr.gov/docs/fy26osti/93846.pdf).
